h: Flag, book and Mahatma: the young have won, now it is the government's call
dek: According to Bikshham Gujja, every label has lost its sting against a generation that has taken to the streets with the Constitution, Gandhi and the tricolour, and now the BJP and the Sangh must choose between saving one officer and saving civil rights.
body: On 6 October, scientist and policy analyst Bikshham Gujja wrote that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar would have to go before the end of October, or the government would move towards an Emergency in one form or another. In this piece he lists what has happened since: the Cockroach Janta Party's nationwide movement from Mumbai on 2 October, the siege of Delhi on 10-11 October and about six hundred arrests in Mumbai, the denotification of Jantar Mantar as a protest site, and Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka being sent to Tihar.

In the writer's view the movement's strength lies in three symbols: the book of the Constitution, Gandhi's non-violent method and the tricolour. The movement began on Gandhi Jayanti, and all three were present at every detention. Arresting a young person holding the flag only hurts the government. Labels like anti-national, foreign money and cockroach have become a joke, so the fear of them is gone too.

Of the movement's three demands, Gujja thinks the third matters most: repeal the 2023 law that removed the Chief Justice from the committee that selects election commissioners and seated a Union minister in his place. In his opinion Gyanesh Kumar is no longer the question; his credibility is already gone. The objections of his own two colleagues on the Commission have come out, and the order for a summary revision in seventeen states looks like a retreat.

He also gives a warning. The left links of AISA president Neha Bora could give the BJP a chance to turn the debate into left versus right, so the movement should keep its aim on the Chief Election Commissioner alone. He suggests reaching out even to BJP and Sangh workers who want clean elections, and building a minimum agenda on conflict of interest, accountability and independent appointments.

The writer concludes that the government has only two paths: sacrifice one officer, or an Emergency with long detentions. In 1977 it was poor voters who defeated Indira Gandhi, because for them having a name cut from the roll is like being declared dead. In his view 26 November, Constitution Day, will show whose side the truth is on. The Commission and the BJP deny any wrongdoing.
nazar: This piece is three weeks old, but its test has come closer. Constitution Day is two weeks away, Gyanesh Kumar is still in his chair, and the Commission is quietly reversing one decision after another. So the writer was right that the retreat has begun; there is just no courage to admit it.

The most useful point is the one about the selection law. Even if one face changes, as long as the government has a majority at the table that picks commissioners, the next Gyanesh Kumar will be ready and waiting.
sawal: Who will be sitting in the Commission's chair by Constitution Day?
ref: The 2023 selection law

The law on appointing the Chief Election Commissioner and commissioners. Its selection committee has the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and a Union minister; the Chief Justice was left out.
Summary revision
The normal yearly correction of the voter roll, in which, unlike SIR, papers are not demanded afresh from every voter.
ank: names cut in the SIR process

h: When fear stops working, the silence breaks
dek: Soumyajit Bhar argues that ten years of public silence rested not just on repression but on the belief that everyone else would also stay quiet, and that the cockroach movement has broken that belief.
body: Soumyajit Bhar, who teaches at BML Munjal University, starts with an old puzzle. Over the last ten years, educated middle-class people said things about the government in private that they never said in public. The writer wants to understand why this private anger did not become public, and why things now seem to be changing.

He says arrests of journalists and activists, pressure on institutions and loosely worded laws do have an effect, but repression alone is not enough. Silence lasts because of a belief that criticism is both dangerous and useless. People act not on their own opinion but on their guess about others. When everyone assumes the rest will stay quiet, the shared anger never shows. In the professional world the fear was less of arrest and more of damage to one's career, online attacks and being declared outside the nation.

The Cockroach Janta Party began with paper leaks, unemployment and failing institutions, and then took on the Election Commission over the revision of the voter roll. The sit-ins went on despite detentions. In the writer's view, sit-ins show people that others will come too. Then joining is no longer a lone risk, and every new person changes everyone else's calculation. He calls this collective efficacy: not a certainty of winning, just a belief that joining is not pointless.

Laughter, satire and memes played a big part. They gave anger a voice and tested whether others thought the same. But the writer also lists three cautions: majoritarian movements can use the same power, successful protests do not turn into lasting organisations on their own, and political parties can swallow a movement even while protecting it. His conclusion is that change begins with recognising that you are not alone, and whether it lasts depends on what is built next.
nazar: This piece opens up the psychological layer behind the slogans, which is often missed. The bigger news than the crowd at Jantar Mantar is that people in offices and on campuses have begun to speak openly.

The warning about parties swallowing the movement is the most urgent one today. After the Ramlila Maidan rally, the question of whose stage this is matters as much to the students as to the government.
sawal: The fear of being alone is broken; who will now build the organisation?
ref: Collective efficacy
A concept in sociology: the shared belief that acting together can make a difference.
Cockroach Janta Party
A youth movement that grew out of a satirical account against paper leaks and unemployment, and is now leading sit-ins against SIR and the Chief Election Commissioner.

h: No algorithm runs the street
dek: According to S N Sahu, the answer to the secret software that cut lakhs of names is a crowd that no code can control.
body: S N Sahu begins in Brazil. When Lula da Silva won in October 2026, a woman's caption went viral: the streets have no algorithm. It meant that people talking to each other, organising and gathering cannot be controlled by any machine, whatever the money, power and technology. The writer applies this to India's SIR.

According to him, in West Bengal a flag called logical discrepancy removed 27 lakh voters a few weeks before the election. A report of 23 September said the Commission's software let officials add or delete names anywhere in the country, when this right belongs only to the Electoral Registration Officer. Commissioners Sukhbir Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had objected and asked for an audit. There were also reports that judges hearing appeals of voters cut in Bengal could not even send notices because of problems with the portal.

The writer's complaint is that how this algorithm works was neither told to the public nor released under the Right to Information. In his view this secrecy gave rise to mass deletions and charges of vote theft. On 1 October the opposition framed six charges against Gyanesh Kumar in a 'people's impeachment', and on 1 November held the 'Save the vote, save the country' rally at Ramlila Maidan. The writer says that no action was taken even on complaints filed under oath by the Biju Janata Dal and the Samajwadi Party.

In the end he goes back to Gandhi and Ambedkar. In 1931 Gandhi called the vote direct action and saw satyagraha as even more powerful. Ambedkar said: educate, agitate, organise. In the writer's view, spontaneous sit-ins full of humour, satire and plain speaking are among the tools that can save the Constitution from the algorithm's attack.
nazar: The machine is the handiest excuse of all: if a name was cut, the system cut it, not a person. The real demand of the piece is that code deciding something like citizenship should be examined in the open.
Until the software is accounted for in public, every fix will be incomplete, and the street will be the only place left where a question can be asked.
sawal: Who will audit the code that runs the voter roll?
ref: Logical discrepancy
A flag put by the software in SIR when details of name, age or family relationship do not match old records.
ERONet / ECINet
The Election Commission's online platforms, where voter roll data is kept and changed.

h: The crowd came; where will the votes come from?
dek: A Navbharat editorial argues that the Ramlila Maidan rally showed opposition unity, but the vote theft issue alone will not win elections.
body: This editorial sees the big INDIA alliance rally led by the Congress at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan as a show of opposition strength, but puts a direct question alongside: will this crowd turn into votes? The writer recalls that this same ground saw Jayaprakash Narayan's Total Revolution rally in 1975, the Janata rally after the Emergency in 1977, and Anna Hazare's movement in 2011.

In the writer's view, the 'Save the vote, save the Constitution' rally, and the symbolic parliament on the lawn of Mallikarjun Kharge's house, chaired by Meira Kumar, which raised the impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, may look theatrical, but they are a planned strategy to stir public opinion. Mamata Banerjee's vote theft campaign in Bengal is described as part of the same effort to win back lost ground.

Then the editorial puts Bihar's numbers on the table. Rahul Gandhi's Voter Adhikar Yatra (voters' rights march) against SIR covered about 1300 kilometres and 20 districts, and there was a big meeting at Patna's Gandhi Maidan, yet the Congress contested 61 seats and won only 6. In the writer's view, schemes like Nitish Kumar's promise of ten thousand rupees to women proved more effective.

The writer advises that the opposition must go beyond the charge of vote theft and build solid social alliances, as the Congress did in Telangana before the election by bringing together Dalits, Adivasis (indigenous communities) and leaders of the separate state movement. The editorial also says that while targeting the Election Commission along with the government and the BJP, the Congress forgets that no legal action can be taken against the Chief Election Commissioner while he holds a constitutional post.
nazar: This editorial raises the question the movement wants to avoid: the power of the street and the power of the ballot box are not the same thing. But there is a tangle in it too. If names are being cut from the voter roll itself, it is hasty to treat an election defeat as proof that the issue is weak. The charge of vote theft is not just an election slogan; it is about the ground on which every election is fought.

And the point that the Chief Election Commissioner cannot be acted against does not go against the movement, it goes in its favour: where no accountability sticks to a post, the street is the last court left.
sawal: Why did the crowd at Gandhi Maidan shrink to six seats?
ref: Total Revolution (Sampoorna Kranti)
Jayaprakash Narayan's movement of 1974-75. The Emergency was imposed on the very night of its Ramlila Maidan rally on 25 June 1975.
Voter Adhikar Yatra
Rahul Gandhi's march against SIR in Bihar, which covered about 1300 kilometres and 20 districts and ended in Patna.

h: Public anger should not be shut inside one resignation
dek: According to Deba Ranjan, the opposition is stuck on Gyanesh Kumar's resignation, when the real question is the whole system that lets one commissioner act arbitrarily.
body: Social activist Deba Ranjan asks whether gathering more than a lakh people in Delhi for one day can be called a movement, and whether it is right to limit people's anger to a demand for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. In his eyes, the conduct of the opposition parties raises many questions.

He recalls history. In 1993 the Narasimha Rao government said a lone Chief Election Commissioner could act arbitrarily. At the time, T N Seshan's independent style was troubling the Congress government. An ordinance of 1 October 1993 created a three-member Commission in which all three had an equal voice, and in 1995 a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court upheld it. In the writer's view the same arbitrariness has returned today, only this time under the patronage of the ruling party, and the cutting of 13 crore voters' names is a bigger fraud than the electoral process itself.

The writer charges that the opposition is showing its strength by gathering crowds, but its leaders want power without taking any personal risk. At Ramlila Maidan on 1 November, no speaker talked about transparency, accountability, democratic selection for constitutional posts, panchayati raj (village self-government) and the gram sabha (village assembly), or decentralising power. The disease, from booth capturing to cutting names, has been there since independence, but the opposition fights people, not the system, so the result will be a change of government, not of the system.

He also makes a concrete suggestion: the opposition should have demanded that Jantar Mantar be freed from the government's grip and become an independent place of protest, where Rohith Vemula's mother, the wrestlers, ex-servicemen and Tamil Nadu's farmers have all sat. In the writer's view the student movement is growing in impact because it is connected to people's feelings, and it should grow on its own strength, apart from party control. The real question is whether citizens will be able to save their constitutional rights.
nazar: This piece is an uncomfortable mirror for the opposition, and a necessary one. A movement resting on one face can cool down the moment that face goes, while the structure that cuts names stays just as it is.

The Seshan episode is worth remembering: the whole argument for a multi-member Commission was that one man should not act arbitrarily. If the objections of two commissioners keep being brushed aside, that reform has stayed on paper.
sawal: After the resignation, what will the movement's next demand be?
ref: T N Seshan vs Union of India (1995)
The Supreme Court ruling that upheld a three-member Election Commission and said the commissioners have equal standing.
Jantar Mantar
An area near Parliament in Delhi that has been a protest site for decades; in October 2026 the Home Ministry removed it from the list of protest sites.

h: Tales of butter theft will not cover up vote theft
dek: In Navbharat's satire column Nishanebaaz, the neighbour counts theft among the sixty-four arts, but the writer replies that the story of Kanha cannot bury the question of vote theft.
body: Navbharat's Nishanebaaz column is, as always, a conversation between a neighbour and the writer. This time the neighbour is upset: how long will Rahul Gandhi keep playing the worn-out record of vote theft, and why does he hurt the Prime Minister's dignity by calling the watchman a thief? He also thinks the attacks on Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar are unfair.

The neighbour's arguments are interesting. According to him, a legal provision protects the Chief Election Commissioner from lawsuits over his decisions even after retirement, and when the draft roll came out before the 2024 election, why did the opposition not object then? So why defame the BJP and the Commission by calling them vote thieves?

The writer answers with a saying: better late than never. Then the neighbour lists the long tradition of theft. The scriptures count theft among the sixty-four arts; in literature there are people who publish others' poems under their own name; in acting, many stars borrowed Dilip Kumar's style; and though Nand Baba's house had nine lakh cows, Kanha stole butter from the gopis' (cowherd women's) homes and denied it when Yashoda asked.

Here the writer stops and says plainly that the issue of vote theft cannot be buried by telling the story of butter theft. He repeats the INDIA alliance's line that the BJP is ruling by stealing votes, and quips that now a film called Vote Thief should be made on the lines of Jewel Thief. Satire does not present proof for either side; it puts the arguments of both sides to the test of laughter.
nazar: The real edge of this satire is in the neighbour's arguments, because those are the very arguments heard every day in TV debates: why didn't you speak earlier, the dignity of the office, legal protection. When the defence of an institution is that it cannot even be sued, it sounds less like a defence and more like a confession.

In myth, theft can be seen with affection; a citizen's vote cannot. Yashoda could question Kanha about his theft. What way is left today for the voter to ask questions? That is the question of this movement.
sawal: Is legal protection a defence or a confession?
ref: Nishanebaaz
The daily satire column of Navbharat, a Hindi newspaper published from Nagpur, written as a conversation between a neighbour and the writer.
Protection for the Chief Election Commissioner
A provision added in the 2023 law that no civil or criminal action can be taken against commissioners for acts done while in office.

h: The ruling side's counter-rally is an admission of weakness
dek: According to Arun Srivastava, the 'Save democracy, remove anarchy' rallies show that the BJP is falling behind in the battle of narratives.
body: Senior journalist Arun Srivastava sees Home Minister Amit Shah's 'Save democracy, remove anarchy' campaign as a ploy meant to paint Rahul Gandhi's sit-ins as a threat to democracy. In his view the Sangh knows that the INDIA alliance's unity is fragile and will find it hard to last until the coming state elections, so this street clash is an attempt to pull the opposition away from electoral ground.

At Ramlila Maidan on 1 November, Rahul Gandhi challenged the Prime Minister to a debate on any stage and said that cutting the names of crores of voters is treason. In reply, Shah called SIR a necessary cleaning of voter data and accused the opposition of protecting infiltrators. In the writer's view Modi has kept avoiding a direct answer, and the counter-rally is a way to suppress the truth.

Under Article 324(5) the government cannot directly remove the Chief Election Commissioner, but the writer says the Prime Minister could have asked for his resignation. In his eyes the reason he did not is that a resignation would amount to admitting the charges, and the government needs Gyanesh Kumar for the 2029 election. This is the writer's guess. He also lists that in the past month the Commission reversed at least six decisions, removed the SIR declaration from the online form, and ordered camps and door-to-door checks for vulnerable groups.

According to the writer, some BJP leaders accept that the party is behind in the battle of narratives for now, especially among young voters, where the old WhatsApp and TV method is working less well. His conclusion is that for a party that holds the administration, the police and the institutions, taking to the streets to 'save democracy' is a contradiction, and a sign of weakness too.
nazar: It always looks odd when those in power stage a protest: if you hold the power to decide, whom are you complaining to? The piece is right to ask this, even if the talk of a 2029 plot is only a guess.
The Commission's reversals show that the pressure is working. Counter-rallies do not reduce that pressure; they only show that the government too is now forced to speak the language of the street.
sawal: Why did those in power need to take to the streets?
ref: Article 324(5)
The constitutional provision under which the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only by a process like that for a Supreme Court judge, that is, impeachment by Parliament.
Save democracy, remove anarchy
The BJP's November 2026 rally campaign in response to the anti-SIR movement.

h: Iran and America: not a first step, but steps taken together
dek: Former Iranian MP Ali Saari says the talks stuck over Hormuz will open only when both sides take small, checkable steps at the same time.
body: For years, talks between Iran and America have kept getting stuck on one question: who bends first? Should Iran first cut its nuclear work and then get relief, or should America first ease the pressure? In the writer's view the real question is not the order, but whether both can move together.

Right now the knot is the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran says it will open the route if America lifts its naval blockade, eases sanctions and guarantees it will not attack again. Iran says there will be no talks under pressure, while Washington wants the nuclear issue on the table from day one.

Saari recalls the interim deal of 2013, which set out small, reversible steps from both sides. Out of it came the 2015 nuclear deal, which capped uranium enrichment at 3.67 percent, increased international monitoring, and lifted sanctions in return. It was also carried out in stages, from the July 2015 agreement to January 2016.

But the lesson of that same deal is also that without a political guarantee, any sequence is weak. In 2018 America walked out and sanctions came back. America argues that relief should come only when Iran's promises can be checked, and critics believe that side-by-side steps are not possible amid such deep mistrust.

The writer suggests opening Hormuz in stages, with a third party watching each stage. Qatar could be the bridge for talks and the International Atomic Energy Agency could handle the nuclear question. The memorandum of understanding reached with Qatar's help in June, and the technical committees formed after it, were a start in this direction.
nazar: If Hormuz stays shut, the first to feel it are the kitchens and fares in oil-buying countries like India, and the livelihoods of lakhs of Indian workers in the Gulf are shaken. So this debate is not just about Tehran and Washington.

In our view Saari's point matters because it leaves the language of winning and losing and talks about a way to build trust. India, which has ties with both, could have openly backed such a step-by-step path, but its voice is almost missing from this debate.
sawal: Who will count each door opened at Hormuz, and whom will both sides trust?
ref: Strait of Hormuz
The narrow sea route between Iran and Oman through which a large share of the world's oil passes. When it closes, oil becomes costlier across the world.
JCPOA (2015)
The nuclear deal between Iran and six major powers, in which Iran limited enrichment in return for sanctions being lifted. America left it in 2018.

h: Hunger is rising in Pakistan, but TV debates are elsewhere
dek: Reports from the World Bank to the UNDP show poverty, hunger and mental distress deepening in Pakistan, but the government claims stability and the media stays silent.
body: Pakistan's government talks of economic stability returning, but according to water governance expert Naseer Memon, recent international reports tell a different story. In World Bank figures, the national poverty rate rose from 22 percent in 2018-19 to 29 percent in 2024-25, which means about seven crore people are below the poverty line. The Gini index, which measures inequality, is also at its highest level in twenty-five years.

Look beyond income and things are worse. In the UNDP's Multidimensional Poverty Index, 38.3 percent of Pakistanis, about nine and a half crore people, are poor on measures of health and education, while the rate is 16.4 percent in India and 14.9 percent in Bangladesh. In the 2026 Global Hunger Index, Pakistan ranks 106th of 122 countries and has the highest hunger score in South Asia.

Memon draws attention to another little-discussed figure. According to a national survey published in the British Medical Journal, every third Pakistani has an identifiable mental or behavioural disorder, and every fifth person showed symptoms of post-traumatic stress (PTSD). These rates were found to be linked to low income, unemployment and poor education.

The writer sees the root in decades of wrong policies. In his view human development has become mere decoration for speeches and manifestos, while security concerns and border tension pull away the money. Farming is breaking under the weight of costly inputs, badly managed water, degrading land and expensive fuel. Food inflation has made many families' plates smaller.

In the end Memon complains about the media. TV channels are busy debating sensational issues like governor's rule and new provinces, while the reports on hunger and poverty are left out of the discussion. In the writer's view, distracting the public will not reduce its anger.
nazar: This piece is not just a mirror for Pakistan. In India too, celebration takes the place of data and emotional issues take the place of hunger in debates, and on both sides of the border security spending eats into the share of bread and schools. The common enemy of ordinary people in South Asia is poverty and malnutrition, not the neighbour.
In our view talk of peace matters also because if tension eases, both countries can spend on farming, water and health.
sawal: Every third citizen is in mental distress, so why is prime time silent?
ref: Multidimensional Poverty Index
A measure by the UNDP and Oxford that counts not just income but also shortfalls in health, education and living standards.
Gini index
A measure of inequality in income or spending. The higher the number, the more unequal the society.

h: Israel's election: Netanyahu lost, but the road still opens for him
dek: According to historian Ilan Pappe, the 27 October results make a new government hard to form, and the time until fresh elections could lead Netanyahu to war again.
body: Many people see Israel's 27 October election as a defeat for Benjamin Netanyahu. Historian Ilan Pappe does not agree. He says that in a system he considers one of apartheid, numbers do not mean what they mean in a normal democracy.

In the 120-seat parliament, Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats. The opposing Jewish bloc and the 19 seats of Palestinian parties together make 67. But a government needs 61, and opposition leaders such as Gadi Eisenkot have refused to take Palestinian parties along. Taking the religious hardline parties along would mean exempting Haredi youth from military service, which goes against Eisenkot's election promise.

A shared government with prime ministers taking turns also does not look possible to Pappe. Netanyahu is facing trial, he cannot become a minister, and in 2020 he played this very game with Benny Gantz and brought the government down.

According to the writer, the most likely outcome is that no government is formed and elections are held again in six months. Meanwhile Netanyahu could reignite war with Iran and Hezbollah and step up action in Gaza and the West Bank. According to Pappe, this path suits Netanyahu also because this time the results were shaped by heavy turnout among Palestinian citizens and liberal Jewish voters who returned from abroad.

Pappe concludes that whoever forms the government, policy on Gaza and the West Bank will not change unless the world makes it pay a clear price. At the same time he believes that the cracks within Jewish society and growing isolation in the world are hollowing out this project in the long run.
nazar: Pappe reminds us that election numbers are not democracy in themselves. In a parliament where parties with 19 seats are kept out before the count for a government even begins, the meaning of a majority changes. In India too, the politics of treating minority representatives as 'untouchable' is not unknown.
It is also worth seeing how the danger of using war as a tool to save power hangs over the whole region, where lakhs of Indians work.
sawal: Where should the voters of the 19 seats that nobody counts go?
ref: Knesset
Israel's 120-member parliament. Forming a government needs the support of 61 members.
Haredi
Israel's ultra-Orthodox Jewish communities; the question of exempting their young men from military service is a big dispute in Israeli politics.

h: The Indus is a living river, not a canal
dek: Syed Khawar Mehdi says Pakistan has come to treat the Indus as a pipeline for delivering water, and the delta, the blind dolphin and the farmers of coastal Sindh are paying the price.
body: Syed Khawar Mehdi's complaint is not with population or development but with a mindset that sees a river only as a means of carrying water. In his view this mindset goes back to British rule, when the Sukkur Barrage widened irrigation in Sindh in 1932. After independence dams, reservoirs, barrages and link canals kept growing, and the illusion took hold that water reaching the sea is wasted.

According to the writer, the delta has taken the biggest blow. The river's fresh water and silt push back the salt water of the sea and keep mangroves and fish alive. As the flow fell, salinity began to reach fields and groundwater, and food security in coastal Sindh came under threat.

The most painful example of this crisis is the bhulan, the nearly blind Indus dolphin that finds its way by echoes of sound. Barrages have broken its world into pieces; it often gets trapped in canals or drowns in nets. The stretch between Guddu and Sukkur is its main refuge, and conservation efforts have brought its numbers back to about two thousand. The barrages have also blocked the upstream journey of the palla fish.

Mehdi sees sewage, factory waste, farm chemicals and plastic as just as big a threat. In his opinion counting the quantity of water and forgetting its quality is accounting cut off from ecology. Electoral thinking likes cutting ribbons on new projects, not maintenance. The clearing of mangroves on the Karachi coast for real estate is part of the same attitude.

His suggestions are clear: environmental flows set on a scientific basis, an account of what downstream areas need, assessment of the impact of projects across the whole basin, treatment of sewage, and a role for riverside communities in decisions.
nazar: This story of the Indus is no different from our Ganga, Narmada and Brahmaputra. In India too, rivers have been reduced to a sum of dams and canals, and the delta's fishers, farmers and river creatures carry the burden.
In our view, before fighting over water across the border, it is necessary to accept that the river too needs its share. Protecting shared rivers could also be a path to peace in South Asia.
sawal: Is water that reaches the sea really wasted?
ref: Indus dolphin (bhulan)
A nearly blind freshwater dolphin found only in the Indus river, which finds its way by echoes. It is an endangered species.
Environmental flow
The minimum water released into a river that is needed to keep its creatures, its delta and the people along its banks alive.

h: Climate summit in Antalya: the hosts themselves are expanding coal
dek: According to Rachel Mellor, there is hope from COP31 only if promises are acted on, while both host countries are themselves expanding fossil fuels.
body: The UN climate summit COP31 began on 9 November in Antalya, Turkey. This time the arrangement is unusual: Turkey is the host and its minister Murat Kurum is president, while Australia's Chris Bowen leads the negotiations. This split was settled at COP30, when the two countries' rival bids had stalled the process.

According to the writer, the summit will be judged on three things: a fair exit from fossil fuels, money for climate, and making cities able to withstand shocks. Kurum himself admits that the world faces a shortfall of 5.6 to 7.1 lakh crore dollars for adaptation, and that money from the loss and damage fund has not yet reached communities on the front line.

The picture is frightening. In 2025 carbon emissions rose 1.1 percent to a new record, August 2026 was 1.65 degrees warmer than before the industrial era, and current policies point to 2.8 degrees of warming by the end of the century. The richest 0.1 percent emit more carbon than about half the world's population. About 50 countries have not submitted new climate plans, among them India, Argentina, Egypt, Iran and Vietnam.

The sharpest point is about the hosts. Australia has approved 37 fossil projects since 2022, including the expansion of a coal mine in the Hunter Valley, and Turkey plans to raise coal and gas capacity by 30 percent by 2035.

Still, the writer sees some hope: a voluntary pledge on electrification, a record 2.3 lakh crore dollars invested in clean energy in 2025, and new disclosure rules for delegates meant to rein in the fossil lobby. But many voices, from Greta Thunberg to Ban Ki-moon, do not think these summits are fit for their purpose.
nazar: India's name among the countries that did not submit a new climate plan on time should trouble us. Demands on rich countries for money and justice carry weight only when one's own homework is done. It is also true that the shortfall in adaptation money falls hardest on those in our country who work under the open sky in heat, floods and drought.
The hosts expanding coal shows that the real crisis is the gap between the summit stage and domestic policy. This gap exists in India too.
sawal: When the hosts are expanding coal, whose decision will carry the table?
ref: COP31
The 31st annual conference of the member countries of the UN climate treaty, being held in Antalya, Turkey, from 9 to 20 November 2026.
Loss and damage fund
An international fund to help poor countries recover from the destruction caused by climate disasters, agreed at COP28.

h: The lesson of left wins: the party machine tames them first
dek: Jawed Naqvi reads one story running from progressive wins in the US midterms to South Asia's left-populist experiments, in which the establishment wins in the end.
body: Dawn's Delhi correspondent Jawed Naqvi begins with America's 2026 midterm elections. James Talarico won in Texas, Annie Andrews in South Carolina and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, and Flanagan became the first Native American woman to reach the Senate. The writer sees the Senate win of Palestine supporter Abdul El-Sayed as a blow to the lobby that spent heavily against him.

But according to Naqvi, a contrary wind is also blowing inside the Democratic Party. In his view Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, who want leadership in the Senate and the House, are deeply tied to the pro-Israel lobby AIPAC and did not speak against arms supplies during the Gaza war. The writer believes this anger fuelled the progressive surge, but there is little hope of democratic socialists winning inside the party.

Then he turns to South Asia. Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's PPP, Indira Gandhi's Congress before the Emergency, Sri Lanka's JVP, Mujibur Rahman's socialist populism and Nepal's communist parties: according to the writer, in all of them left idealism finally had to struggle against the pressure of the power establishment.

In India he judges Rahul Gandhi's left-populist turn by the same test. Attacks on crony capitalism, a caste census, talk of redistributing wealth, rural distress and youth unemployment are on his agenda. But according to Naqvi, the pull between generations and dependence on corporate donations make this road hard.

He describes the PPP of Benazir Bhutto's time as something like the 'Third Way' of Blair and Clinton, which embraced the market and reassured the elite and Washington. He also criticises the JVP for striking a deal with the IMF and adopting soft diplomatic language on Israel.
nazar: Naqvi's lesson is for India's opposition too. Talking of equality and justice on the campaign stage is easy; once in power, taking on corporate donations and old foreign policy habits is hard.
In our view promises of a caste census and jobs will inspire trust only when parties also change their own internal structure; otherwise every surge will end as one more disillusionment.
sawal: If the donors are unhappy, how long will left promises last?
ref: JVP
Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna, a left party in Sri Lanka that was once linked to armed uprisings and has now reached power through electoral politics.
AIPAC
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, an influential pro-Israel lobby in the US that spends money for and against candidates in elections.

h: Dalit youth killed in Vaijapur: demand for a CBI probe
dek: After the killing of Rohit Pathare, Bahujan groups have demanded a fast-track court, a CBI investigation and the suspension of police officers.
body: The Vanchit Bahujan Aghadi and the All India Panther Sena have taken up the killing of Dalit youth Rohit Anil Pathare in Vaijapur, in Maharashtra's Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district. Both groups are demanding a trial in a fast-track court, a CBI investigation, the suspension of the police officers responsible and strict punishment for the accused.

According to the report, on 31 October, during the Ganesh festival, a fight broke out between two Ganesh mandals (festival committees) over an old feud. The family alleges that about 26 people dragged Rohit from his home to a field near Rotegaon, tied him to a tree, attacked him with swords, iron rods and an axe, and urinated in his mouth when he asked for water. He died in a hospital in Shirdi on 3 November.

The family also alleges that office-bearers linked to the BJP were among the attackers and that the local police at first tried to shield the accused. Rohit's mother even tried to set herself on fire at the police station. On the complaint of his wife Sheetal Pathare, a case has been registered against 26 people under sections on murder and the Atrocities Prevention Act.

The police formed five teams and 16 accused have been caught so far, including the main accused. Six more arrests were made on 9 November, but several accused are still absconding. Sanjay Shirsat, the minister in charge of the district, announced help of five lakh rupees for the family.

The Panther Sena has demanded that MCOCA be applied and that the role of about 150 people from the lane be investigated, and has warned of a statewide agitation. The Vanchit Bahujan Aghadi compared this killing to the Khairlanji massacre and said the family is living in the shadow of fear.
nazar: A killing in which the accused number more than two dozen is not a sudden flare-up but the open boldness of a mob. And this boldness comes when the attackers are confident that the police station will stand with them.
Arrests and compensation are necessary, but the real test is whether accountability is fixed for the police's early laxity, and whether the family gets a setting in which it can testify without fear.
sawal: Who will finally take responsibility for the safety of the Dalit family?
ref: Atrocities Prevention Act
A 1989 law that treats caste violence against Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe people as a separate crime and provides for speedy trials in special courts.
Khairlanji massacre
In 2006, in Khairlanji village of Maharashtra's Bhandara district, a mob brutally killed four members of a Dalit family.

h: Kerala's sports AI: no tender, and children's data at stake
dek: An 80 lakh rupee AI platform for sports data is being given to a startup through direct purchase, and its oversight committee has not a single technology or privacy expert.
body: Kerala's sports and youth affairs department is getting an AI and data analytics platform called 'Game Keralam' built, which will bring the state's government sports data together in one place. This will include records of minor athletes too. The total cost has been set at 80 lakh rupees, of which the government will give 50 lakh and the remaining 30 lakh is to come from CSR and partnerships.

According to the report, the work is being given without an open tender, through direct purchase, to a startup recognised by the Kerala Startup Mission. A 2022 government order had raised the limit for direct purchase from such startups from 20 lakh to 50 lakh. Keeping the government's share at exactly 50 lakh is seen as using this provision. Critics and people linked to the industry have questioned its transparency.

A five-member review committee has been formed for oversight, and all of its members are officials of the department. It has no independent technology expert, no one who knows data architecture and no privacy expert.

According to experts, handling children's data needs verified parental consent, and the law bars tracking children and building profiles of them based on behaviour. The platform is to run in the state's own data centre, which needs costly GPUs, and experts find this hard within an 80 lakh budget. Grassroots sports records are scattered across paper and spreadsheets, and sports associations are not legally bound to hand over their data.
The report records no response from the department, the minister or the startup.
nazar: Every government wants to look modern by invoking AI, but when the matter is children's personal data, the first question should be about safety and consent, not shine.

Without a tender and without independent experts, such a project puts both public money and children's privacy at risk. The government should make this contract and the make-up of the committee public.
sawal: Who will take responsibility for protecting children's data?
ref: Direct purchase
An exemption under government rules that allows purchases up to a set limit to be made directly from a recognised vendor, without open bidding.
Verified parental consent
A condition of the data protection law that firm, checked permission from parents must be taken before collecting a child's personal data.

h: Tidigol: Dalits attacked at a jatra, a march for justice
dek: Dalit youths were attacked for joining a temple procession in Tidigol village in Raichur, and thousands gathered in Sindhanur despite prohibitory orders.
body: On 18 October, in Tidigol village of Sindhanur taluk in Karnataka's Raichur district, Dalit youths trying to join the procession of the Anjaneya temple jatra (village fair) were stopped. According to the report, when they protested they were brutally attacked and a mob chased them all the way to the Dalit settlement. Women and elderly people who came to intervene were also beaten, and several injured were admitted to hospital in Sindhanur.

It is alleged that, on the contrary, a counter-case was also filed against the Dalits, and the local police sided with the attackers instead of the victims. Two weeks later the main accused are said to still not have been caught, though minister Ajay Singh had reported six arrests. Out of fear, some Dalit families left the village.
In early November the district's deputy commissioner and officials held peace meetings in the village, after which Dalits were allowed to enter the temple and worship.

On 8 November a federation of Dalit and progressive organisations called for 'Chalo Tidigol' (march to Tidigol). The administration banned meetings and rallies within five kilometres of the village and deployed heavy police. Despite this, thousands of workers, farmers, women and students gathered at Ambedkar Circle in Sindhanur. The police stopped the march from going to the village, and the additional superintendent of police assured them the demands would be seriously considered.
The protesters' demands are: arrest of all the accused, withdrawal of false cases filed against Dalits, and safety for the community.
nazar: An attack over trying to walk along in a temple procession shows that equality in the village is still a fight, not something taken for granted. Entry into the temple after the peace meeting is a good start, but it does not settle the account for that violence.
When a counter-case is filed against the victims of an attack and prohibitory orders are imposed on those seeking justice, questions about the administration's priorities are bound to arise.
sawal: Why prohibitory orders for the victims, and leniency for the attackers?
ref: Jatra
The annual fair of the village deity in Karnataka and nearby regions, with a procession of a chariot or palanquin.
BNSS Section 163
A section of the new criminal procedure code under which the district administration can impose a temporary ban on meetings and processions in an area.

h: Hasina asks for a passport, Dhaka says extradition first
dek: Bangladesh has rejected an application sent on Sheikh Hasina's behalf for a passport and identity card, and said she can return only through extradition.
body: An application has come in for a new passport and national identity card for Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina. The British law firm Matrix Chambers made the request by email to Bangladesh's High Commission in New Delhi on 9 November. Dhaka has flatly refused.

The High Commission's press minister Mohammad Saidur Rahman said the email came with no paper showing that Hasina had given the firm this work, so the application was sent on to the foreign ministry. An official of the ministry says a passport is a facility given by the government, not a right, and for extradition a one-way travel pass is issued, which can be given only after the legal process in India is complete.

Minister of state for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir called the application absurd and called Hasina a terrorist. He alleges that Hasina fled after more than 1,500 people died. He said she should return, appear before the court and serve her sentence.

Hasina has been in India since the mass uprising of August 2024. In November 2025 the International Crimes Tribunal sentenced her to death in her absence. Dhaka has been seeking her extradition since December 2024. Recently Hasina said she wants to return in December.
Her diplomatic passport was cancelled in August 2024, and in February 2025 the Election Commission blocked the identity cards of her and nine members of her family.
nazar: This passport application looks like a paper move, but in fact it puts the ball in India's court. Hasina is in Delhi and India has to decide on extradition, which means a hard test of our relationship with a neighbour is standing at our door.
Justice demands an accounting for those killed in the uprising, but a death sentence handed down in absence also raises questions. The line between revenge and justice will be tested right here.
sawal: Who will give an identity to someone the country has already sentenced to death?
ref: Extradition treaty 2013
The agreement between India and Bangladesh on handing over criminals. Political offences are outside it, but crimes like murder are not automatically treated as political.
International Crimes Tribunal
A domestic court of Bangladesh that tries crimes against humanity. It is the court that sentenced Hasina.

h: Library book scam: High Court says name those responsible
dek: The Madras High Court has ordered the vigilance department to register an FIR over irregularities in the purchase of books for Tamil Nadu's public libraries.
body: The Madurai bench of the Madras High Court has told Tamil Nadu's Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption to register an FIR over irregularities in the purchase of books for public libraries. The bench of Justice G R Swaminathan and Justice M D Sumathi was hearing a contempt petition alleging that the government had not followed a court order of June 2024.

The judges said the wrongdoing came to light after an article by Tamil writer Perumal Murugan. Justice Swaminathan told library director R V Shajeevana not to try to shield anyone, to give the names of the officers responsible by the next day, and that the bank accounts of the publishers facing charges should be frozen. He also asked who had recommended buying the publications of 'Agal Vilakku'.

The case began in 2019 with a petition by S Krishnan of Nagercoil. The charge was that publishers were reprinting old books under new titles and new authors' names to win fresh government orders, including books out of copyright and nationalised books. The rule says the same book cannot be bought again within five years.

In June 2024 the court had called it a scam and ordered a transparent purchase policy, a list of the selected books on the website and an inquiry committee. The government counsel said a complaint was sent on 6 November and the investigation began on 7 November.
nazar: Village and small-town libraries are often the poor reader's only window. If old books reach them in new clothes, the theft is not only of money but of readers' trust and writers' identity.
It is also worth noting that the scam was exposed by a writer's pen, not by any government inquiry. The court had warned back in 2024, yet nothing happened for two years.
sawal: An old book with a new name: whom should the reader ask?
ref: Perumal Murugan
A well-known Tamil novelist. In 2015, after protests, he announced the 'death' of the writer in him, and later began writing again after a Madras High Court ruling.
Nationalised books
The Tamil Nadu government has bought the rights to the works of many writers and opened them to the public, so that anyone can print them.

h: Drive drunk and lose your licence, no need to wait for the trial
dek: The Kerala High Court has said that officials do not need to wait for a criminal verdict to cancel the licences of those who drive after drinking.
body: The Kerala High Court has said that in drunk driving cases, the licensing authority can decide on its own on the basis of the evidence before it. It does not need to wait until the criminal trial is over. Justice Kauser Edappagath said this with reference to Section 19(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act.

The case was the bail plea of a man accused of driving a car rashly after drinking, killing a motorcyclist. The court granted him bail because he had no criminal record, but told the investigating officer to send his licence to the licensing authority for action.

The judge was concerned that drunk driving cases are rising, yet this power is very rarely used, which weakens the fear of the law. The court recalled the Supreme Court's 2014 direction that licences be suspended for at least three months in cases such as driving drunk, speeding and talking on the phone while driving.

The transport commissioner was directed that the motor vehicles department act at once in such cases. Where drink appears at first sight to be the cause of an accident, the licensing authority should consider disqualifying the driver or cancelling the licence without delay.
nazar: Most of those killed in road accidents are pedestrians, cyclists and two-wheeler riders, who have neither clout nor lawyers. Trials go on for years, and until then the accused is back driving on the same road. The court's stand is an attempt to bridge that gap.
But there is also a risk that this power is used only against a select few. The real test will be whether the same strictness is shown to big cars and big people too.
sawal: The motorcyclist is gone; why is the licence still in his pocket?
ref: Section 19(1), Motor Vehicles Act
Gives the licensing authority the power to cancel the licence of, or disqualify, a dangerous or habitually careless driver.
S Rajaseekaran vs Union of India
A 2014 Supreme Court case in which states were given several directions on road safety, including licence suspension.

h: The village Diwali: a mountain of cow dung, Sohrai on the walls
dek: City Diwali is limited to lamps and firecrackers, but in villages the same season is a festival of harvest, cattle, ancestors and folk deities.
body: Across a large part of the country, Diwali means Lakshmi puja, lamps and fireworks. But in villages this season is tied to the harvest, and cattle, ancestors and the deities who guard the village are remembered in it.

The day after Diwali is Govardhan puja, also called Annakoot. In many homes in Braj, Rajasthan and Gujarat, a Govardhan hill is made of cow dung and heaps of food are offered on it. Ritu Singh of Pithrawas in Haryana says that in her home a cow-dung idol of Krishna has been made for generations, and after the puja it is a calf that breaks it. In the Jangalmahal region of Jharkhand and Bengal, the Kurmi community celebrates Bandna, in which cattle are bathed and decorated and farm tools are worshipped.

The Santhal community celebrates Sohrai from the day after Diwali. Hazaribagh is its best-known centre, where married women plaster walls with mud, cow dung and husk and paint animals, leaves and vines on them. According to Geeta Kumari of Getalsud, every household paints what it knows. Sohrai and Khovar paintings got a GI tag in 2020, but the tradition is fading as houses become pucca (brick and cement).

The Gonds of Chhattisgarh make clay idols of Gaura-Gauri at Devari and take out a wedding procession, in memory of the first Gond wedding. In the Trans-Giri area of Himachal's Sirmaur and in Uttarakhand's Jaunsar-Bawar, Diwali comes a month later as Budhi Diwali (old Diwali), in which, according to the article, more than three lakh Hattee people take part.

The economy of this season also runs from the village. A big share of potters' yearly income comes in these few weeks, but potters in Palamu say clay and fuel have become costlier and there is competition from factory-made lamps. Electric wheels are available, but they also need help with clay and wood.
nazar: This piece reminds us how much diversity is hidden when a single form of a festival is made national. The cow-dung hill, the mud walls and the calf's role show that the worship here is of the labour and livestock on which farming rests.

But these traditions depend on things that are vanishing fast: mud houses, village clay, cattle and the potter's trade. A GI tag is not enough; unless the livelihoods of potters and craftspeople are saved, these festivals will survive only in photographs.
sawal: Into whose hands is the market for lamps going?
ref: Sohrai
The harvest festival of the Santhal and other Adivasi (indigenous) communities of Jharkhand. Women paint pictures with natural colours on the mud walls of their homes.
Budhi Diwali
A Diwali celebrated about a month after Diwali in some hill areas of Himachal and Uttarakhand, with dancing while carrying torches.

h: The Bastar haat: where the forest comes down to market
dek: In Bastar's roughly 300 haats (weekly markets), red ant chutney, rice liquor and bamboo shoots are sold, and most stalls are run by women, but the market is changing too.
body: About 300 weekly haats are held in Bastar. Adivasis gather leaves, flowers, tubers and insects from the forest and bring what is left over to the haat. Near Jagdalpur, three haats can be seen in a week: Pamela on Sunday, Tokapal on Monday and Pakhnar on Tuesday.

The Pamela haat is run mostly by women. They sell rice rotis, bamboo shoots and everyday goods, while men mostly come to sell cows or bet on cockfights. Three things are in the highest demand: chapda, a spicy chutney of red ants and their eggs that is believed to help with fever; landa, a milky liquor made from rice; and liquor made from mahua flowers.

Bindu, founder of the travel startup Culture Devi, says most of the sellers are women and the whole trade in local drinks is run by women. According to Pallavi Dehari, a young Adivasi from Bastar, whatever happens in the region, the haats have survived; they connect scattered villages, and identity, friendship and relationships are formed here.

Tokapal is the biggest and most organised haat. People come on foot, by bus or in packed jeeps. Among jaggery, dried mahua, meat and dried fish, there is also rasam made from jaggery. Ghadwa artisans sell bell-metal figures and jewellery made by wax casting. Pakhnar is mostly a wholesale market, where soap, cold drinks and packaged food are sold.

Change is visible: plastic boxes sit beside hand-woven baskets, and young sellers are giving up barter and buying with cash. According to the writer, mahua, sal leaves, wild mushrooms and ants all depend on the health of the forest, and climate change and shrinking forests threaten them.
nazar: Bastar often comes into the news through the lens of conflict and security. This piece shows its everyday life, where women are the pivot of the market and the forest is kitchen, medicine and income.

But the piece is written from a tourism point of view, and that is also its limit. The haats will survive only if the Adivasis' rights over the forest survive; mines and felled forests could make chapda and mahua vanish before any tourist's photograph does.
sawal: Will the haat survive if the forest itself does not?
ref: Chapda
A spicy chutney made in Bastar from red ants and their eggs, believed to be effective against fever.
Ghadwa art
Bastar's tradition of metal casting, in which molten metal is poured into clay moulds to make figures and jewellery.

h: After the Trishuli flood: where should Nepal resettle?
dek: Al Jazeera's 101 East film looks at Nepal's struggle to save lives and rebuild settlements that were wiped out.
body: 101 East, Al Jazeera's weekly documentary series, released a film of about 25 minutes on Nepal on 7 November. According to the film's introduction, it brings out the efforts being made to save lives and rebuild ruined settlements after a terrible natural disaster.

The disaster struck on the morning of 26 August 2026. A large mass of rock and ice broke off a mountain near Langtang Lirung and came down into the Trishuli river as a fast stream of debris. At first it was thought to be a flood from a glacial lake bursting, but experts later described it as a debris flow formed by a rock and ice avalanche. The debris travelled about a hundred kilometres down the river.

There was destruction in the Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan districts, and the Gyirong area of Tibet across the border was also hit. By early October more than 1,400 deaths had been recorded in Nepal and more than five thousand people were missing. Thousands of homes, schools, health centres, bridges and a large part of the road linking Kathmandu to the Chinese border were swept away.

More than twenty thousand army, armed police and police personnel were deployed for relief, and thousands of people were evacuated. The existing warning system was built for monsoon floods, so this disaster was beyond its reach, and the monitoring stations upstream were also washed away. The cost of rebuilding has been estimated in billions of dollars.

The question of resettlement is the hardest. Khalte village in Rasuwa had been chosen to resettle families displaced by the 2015 earthquake, even though later geological assessments had marked it as a danger zone. This flood almost wiped it out. The government is now talking of building a new town on safe land and treating weak land along the river as unfit to live on.

This is the heart of the film: the long work after the rescue, in which schools, hospitals, roads and livelihoods must come back along with homes. For mountain families who were picked up and resettled elsewhere after one disaster, the question has now arisen a second time: where is safe land, and who will decide it?
nazar: In the Himalaya, disaster is no longer weather news; it is a question about the map of development. Khalte's story shows that despite warnings of danger, homeless people were settled where land was cheap and the decision easy. If rehabilitation again happens in the same hurry, the address of the next disaster will already be written.

It is a mirror for India's Uttarakhand and Sikkim too, where dams, roads and settlements along rivers are growing at the same speed. In fast-warming mountains, warning systems, distance from the river and the views of the displaced all have to be kept together.
sawal: Who should decide the right to resettle those uprooted twice?
ref: 101 East
Al Jazeera English's weekly documentary series, which makes ground-level films on the people and issues of the Asia-Pacific.
Debris flow
A fast flow of broken rock, ice, soil and water from a mountain, which comes down with far more force than an ordinary flood and sweeps away settlements in its path.

h: Trying to take Bhagat Singh off the pedestal and read him
dek: On Sammukh, Yatish Kumar has read Ashok Kumar Pandey's book 'Hinsa-Ahinsa aur Bhagat Singh' (Violence, Non-violence and Bhagat Singh) as an inquiry that takes on the made-up stories of both the right and the left.
body: Poet and prose writer Yatish Kumar says he understands history best through literature. His review, published on Sammukh, is of Ashok Kumar Pandey's book 'Hinsa-Ahinsa aur Bhagat Singh'. According to him, the book breaks the flat split of Gandhi versus Bhagat Singh and examines the exaggerated stories told by both the right and the Communist Party.

The reviewer says the book begins with the autobiography of his uncle Ajit Singh and traces the family's roots to the history of Punjab, 1857, the Arya Samaj and the Ghadar movement. Jallianwala Bagh, the First World War and Lala Lajpat Rai's National College come in as the ground on which a young man's mind was shaped. The writer also gets to the bottom of where the famous story of 'I am sowing guns' came from.

What Yatish likes most is that Pandey is in no hurry to pass judgement and lets readers think for themselves. The book also pauses on the double standards towards women within the revolutionary groups: the role of Durga Bhabhi, the relationship of Yashpal and Prakashvati, and, according to the reviewer, Prakashvati's jewellery, which was sold to raise money for making bombs.

The book presents the Assembly bomb case as a bomb that was never made to kill. It places Jatin Das's hunger strike in the category of non-violent struggle. Bhagwati Charan Vohra's essay is described not as blind support for violence but as an attempt at balance between the two.

The reviewer also lists some gaps. According to the review, the book mentions an invitation from Moscow but does not fully resolve that ideological pull. Azad's attempt to meet Nehru a few weeks before the hanging is left untouched, and the crowd of references sometimes hides the main argument.
nazar: Bhagat Singh is on every party's poster today, and every poster cuts out one piece of him and throws away the rest. So a book that reads him not as a god but as a young man who thought and changed, whose comrades included women and whose group had debates, is useful.

It is easy to split violence and non-violence into two enemy camps. What is hard is accepting that the revolutionary on hunger strike and the satyagrahi going to jail were wrestling with the same question.
sawal: A bomb that took no life: whom was it thrown to be heard by?
ref: Naujawan Bharat Sabha
A youth organisation formed in Lahore in 1926, in which people like Bhagat Singh and Bhagwati Charan Vohra were active. It was a platform for open political campaigning.
HSRA
The Hindustan Socialist Republican Association, formed in 1928 out of the older HRA. 'Socialist' was added to the name, but according to the review the basic principles stayed the same.
photo_note: A young scholar, Mir Sayyid Ali

h: A novel reviewed in the voice of a thief
dek: On Hindwi's Bela, poet Pawan Karan has written his review of Udayan Vajpeyi's novel 'Qayas' (Conjecture) in the voice of the very thief at whose hands a man loses his life in the novel.
body: A book is usually reviewed by standing outside it. Writing on Udayan Vajpeyi's novel 'Qayas', Pawan Karan has taken the opposite road. He gets into the skin of the novel's narrator, a thief who, during a break-in, unknowingly takes the life of a man named Sudeep.

This thief keeps explaining that he came to steal, not to kill, and kept a weapon only to defend himself. He learned this trick from Hindi detective books, which, he says, made him more sensitive. Now death follows him. He imagines confessing to the police. Only three people know his truth: himself, the reader and the writer.

In this same voice Pawan Karan also complains to the writer. At the first event after Sudeep's death, his daughter Nua reads what her father wrote, and the thief sits in the audience weeping, but the writer does not even look his way. According to the reviewer, the novel leaves this character emotionally alone.

Between Sudeep and Vandana there is an unspoken bond that the novel never names. Pawan Karan praises this restraint. Vandana learns to think in Sudeep's company, but her family's suspicion separates her from her friend Sneha. Sushila opposes her confinement and sees her own condition in it.

After praising the images of sunlight, voices and wind, the review arrives at an interesting question: is the writer not also a kind of thief, who takes from the world and escapes punishment? It ends on two unfulfilled wishes of the thief, one of them Vandana's comb that had once fallen into Sudeep's hands.
nazar: This game of reviewing is not just cleverness. By speaking in the character's voice, Pawan Karan shows what straight criticism would miss: whom the novel sees and whom it leaves unseen.
And calling the writer a thief also touches an old unease in Hindi, the sense that literature takes something from other people's lives. The question is what it gives them back.
sawal: If the writer is a thief, which court does he answer to?
ref: Udayan Vajpeyi
A Hindi poet, fiction writer and essayist who lives in Bhopal. He is known for experimental prose and writing on art.
Bela
The blog section of Hindwi, the Hindi platform of the Rekhta Foundation, where essays, reviews, memoirs and columns are published daily.

h: Bengal's Diwali: a lamp before the goddess of darkness
dek: In her column 'C/O Bengal', Baby Shaw explains why Bengal worships Kali instead of Lakshmi on Diwali night, and what kind of tradition of finding light in darkness this is.
body: In most of north India, Diwali is Lakshmi's night. In Bengal it is Kali's night. Baby Shaw writes in her column on Hindwi's Bela that the Bengali mind does not see light as separate from darkness. Standing in deep darkness and lighting a lamp is the meaning of this festival.

The piece shows Kali's homely side through two folk tales. In one, the devotional poet Ramprasad Sen is mending a broken fence alone when a girl like his daughter comes and lends a hand, while his real daughter was inside the house. In the other, a poor bangle seller puts conch-shell bangles on a girl whose priest father says he has no daughter at all. According to the writer, this is Bengal's special quality: the goddess lives in the family as daughter and mother.

In the Shakta tradition the goddess is the source of all the energy of creation. Kali's black colour stands for endless void and time, and Shiva lying beneath her feet for the bond between consciousness and power. According to the writer, a text of 1699 mentions Kali puja at Diwali, in the eighteenth century King Krishnachandra of Nadia promoted it, and then Kalighat, Dakshineswar and Tarapith became its great centres.

From the songs of Ramprasad and Kamalakanta to Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, and from Bankim's 'Anandamath' to modern painters, Kali has kept returning in many forms. Baby Shaw says Bengal's real wealth is ideas, language and the courage to question, so it prays not for riches but for the removal of ignorance.
In the end the piece leaves an uncomfortable question: how much does a society that sees the goddess as the greatest power respect its own women?
nazar: The pressure to celebrate Diwali in a single way is growing: one goddess, one colour, one market. So it is necessary to remember that in this country the same night belongs to different deities in different regions, and this plurality is our heritage.
The piece's last question weighs more than the whole piece. Cheers for Kali in the temple and a woman's silence at home can go together, and often do.
sawal: In a home that cheers for Kali, how much can a woman speak?
ref: Shakta tradition
The stream of Hinduism in which the goddess, or Shakti, is seen as the root of creation. It has deep roots in Bengal, Assam and Odisha.
Ramprasad Sen
An eighteenth-century Bengali devotional poet whose Kali songs are called 'Ramprasadi' and are still sung today.
photo_note: Between shadow and light, Gaganendranath Tagore

h: A day in Jamshedpur that outweighed many days
dek: Mamta Sharma's new story on Sammukh, 'Ek misra hi kaafi hai' (One line is enough), is about a woman alone in a crowd and a meeting that lasts one day.
body: Mamta Sharma's stories have appeared in magazines such as Hans, Kathadesh, Vagarth, Parikatha and Ajkal, and three collections of her stories have come out. Sammukh has published her new story 'Ek misra hi kaafi hai', which takes place entirely within one day.

The story's heroine is unnamed. She feels alone even in a crowd, and she has grown used to hearing that her loneliness is her own choice and that love is only for poets and storytellers. One afternoon she is sitting alone in a quiet restaurant when a man comes and sits at her table, as if he had been looking for her for a long time.

The talk is small: the menu, the soup she likes, the colour of her clothes, which he had already guessed. He holds her hand, and that touch dissolves years of loneliness. Both feel they kept missing each other again and again. The woman weeps and says she fears he will leave again. He promises to return and asks her to wait too.
After the meal the two wander aimlessly through the Bistupur market. He wants to buy her a pink chiffon sari. The evening fades on a bench under an old tree, as the birds return to the branches.

There is no big twist in the story, and that is its strength. Jamshedpur here is not just a place but the heroine's favourite city, which becomes part of this meeting. The full story can be read on Sammukh.
nazar: That living one full day in a rushing life is now a subject for a story is itself a comment on our times. Mamta Sharma sees love not as drama but as attention: someone remembering the soup you like.
In Hindi stories from small towns, a woman's loneliness often comes as a complaint. Here it comes as the hope of a meeting, which is no small thing.
sawal: Can one full day cut through years of loneliness?
ref: Misra
One line of a sher (couplet) in Urdu poetry. Two misras make a sher.
Bistupur
An old and well-known market area of Jamshedpur, the city's main place for shopping and strolling.
photo_note: Meeting on the stairs, Gaganendranath Tagore

h: The fifteen-minute meme and the open-mouthed citizen
dek: An extract from Sudhanva Deshpande's new book, which tries to understand painter Orijit Sen's online political art and its risks.
body: Sudhanva Deshpande, a theatre worker with Jana Natya Manch and managing editor of LeftWord Books, has written a book on painter Orijit Sen, 'Impostor: The Playful Subversions of Orijit Sen'. The Wire has published an extract from it about Sen's political art on social media.

According to the writer, these pictures by Sen are full of jokes, wordplay and hints. He borrows the language of advertising and election campaigns and turns it upside down. A picture may be made in fifteen minutes, most in half an hour to forty-five minutes, and often they spread far and wide within a few hours. His work for a living carries on alongside.

Sen now works almost entirely digitally. Even his large installations at places like the Kochi Biennale were made on a computer and then printed. The writer says Sen's targets sometimes include the Congress and sometimes the left too, but most of the pictures are about the RSS, the BJP and Prime Minister Modi.

At first Sen did not put his name on his pictures. When his work began to appear on posters without credit, he made a mark of a dice with O and S written on it. Deshpande sees this not as a stamp for earning but as a way of taking responsibility: every new post is like throwing the dice, with the risk of arrest or trouble.

The writer also says plainly that Sen comes from an upper-caste Hindu family and is educated and well connected. The extract ends on the question of whether such people will use their standing to stand with the movements of students, farmers, Adivasis, Dalits and workers.
nazar: This extract goes beyond praising the art. Deshpande does not hide his subject's privileges, and this honesty is what makes the writing trustworthy.

In an age when a cartoon can lead to a court case, putting your name on your picture is itself a statement. The question is not only about the artist's courage but also about the society that creates this risk.
sawal: Will privileged artists put their privilege at stake?
ref: Meme
A short picture or line that spreads fast on the internet, often with satire or a joke.
Orijit Sen
A well-known Indian graphic artist whose 'River of Stories' is considered the country's first graphic novel.
photo_note: The rising son-in-law of Bengal, a satirical drawing by Gaganendranath Tagore

h: The ustad's mirror and the training of a singer
dek: An essay by thumri singer Vidya Rao that travels from a small mirror placed by her teacher to music, theatre and Sufi thought.
body: Vidya Rao, a singer of thumri, dadra and ghazal, writes a column called 'Chashma-e-Hunar' (Spring of Art) in The India Forum. This time the essay is on seena-ba-seena training, that is, learning from heart to heart between teacher and student, which has no syllabus and no exam, and where the lesson often comes in the form of a riddle.

The writer was learning from tabla ustad (master) Dayam Ali Qadri how the shifting moods of thumri rise with the tabla and the voice. One afternoon the ustad placed a small, worn shaving mirror in front of her and told her to sing to her reflection. Vidya Rao has been searching for the meaning of this lesson for years.

In this search she goes to the theatre, where Anuradha Kapur would make actors copy one another until you could not tell who was leading. Then she recalls what her guru Naina Devi told her: in the salons of the tawaifs (courtesan singers), big mirrors were extra eyes for the head of the house and the singer. Who came, who left, who was misbehaving, all of it showed in them, and every gathering also became practice.

In Kathakali, after a long make-up session, the performer looks at himself in a small mirror, and at that moment the character enters him. The writer wonders whether the ustad wanted the heroine of the thumri to settle in her in the same way.

The essay goes on to Ibn Arabi, Mir Dard, the goddess tradition, Nandikeshvara's 'Abhinaya Darpana' (Mirror of Gesture) and the Zen mirror. In the end the writer admits she may never fully understand this lesson, and in Kabir's words, this is the seed given by the guru, which takes a lifetime to open.
nazar: In an age of speed and certificates, this essay reminds us that some skills come only slowly and through trust. The ustad's mirror was not a trick but a new way of listening and seeing.
The mention of the mirrors in the salons matters too. The writer records with respect the wisdom and discipline of a tradition that was long called shameful.
sawal: Can slow training survive in a hurried age?
ref: Seena-ba-seena
The tradition of learning directly from the ustad by living with him and listening, in which company matters more than books.
Nukkodi
The small hand mirror looked into after make-up in Kathakali, a sign that the character is complete.
photo_note: Woman playing the veena, Raja Ravi Varma
